Two ways a star burns hydrogen: which one powers the Sun, and which hotter stars?

About: the proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle, and how steeply each rate rises with the central temperature

About this simulation

On screen
The energy generation rates per unit mass εpp (yellow) and εCNO (blue) against the central temperature T, both axes logarithmic, in units of εpp at the centre of the Sun. A dot on each line marks the chosen T, with a thin vertical line through both and a tick at the centre of the Sun, 1.6×10⁷ K. When Z or X changes, the previous line stays faint and dashed. The inset shows the core, flashing at a fixed rate of about ten a second; each flash is yellow (p–p chain) or blue (CNO cycle) with probabilities equal to each process's share of the energy.
Controls
Central temperature T from 1.0×10⁷ to 3.0×10⁷ K; metal fraction Z from 0.002 to 0.04 on a logarithmic scale; hydrogen fraction X from 0.35 to 0.75.
Measured
The rates follow εpp ∝ ρX²T⁴ and εCNO ∝ ρXZT²⁰, calibrated to be equal at 2.0×10⁷ K for X = 0.70, Z = 0.02; ρ cancels. The CNO share is εCNO/(εpp + εCNO). The sidebar Readouts give T, both rates, their ratio and the CNO share.
Conditions
The fixed exponents 4 and 20 hold only near these temperatures: they come from the Gamow peak and fall slowly as T rises (for CNO, about 18 at 2 × 107 K). The CNO cycle is assumed to have reached its steady state, and the calibration puts the crossing at 2.0 × 107 K; textbooks quote between about 1.7 and 2 × 107 K, depending on the composition and rate formulae. The share at the Sun's centre (about 3 per cent here) is larger than the Sun's total, about 1 per cent, because the rest of the core is cooler.
Two Ways to Burn Hydrogen
Energy generation ratesεpp and εCNO against T, log–log

Guided Inquiry

1 · The Sun's CNO share

The sim is set to X = 0.70, Z = 0.02 and a central temperature of 1.6 × 107 K, the temperature at the centre of the Sun. The gas contains all the carbon, nitrogen and oxygen the CNO cycle needs, and the catalysts are never used up. Before looking at the flashes or the readouts, predict what share of the Sun's energy the CNO cycle supplies.

2 · A ten per cent hotter core

Keep the settings of question 1. You will raise the central temperature by ten per cent, from 1.6 × 107 to 1.76 × 107 K. Before dragging, predict by roughly what factors the two rates grow. Then drag and read the dots against the vertical axis.

3 · Where the lines cross

Keep X = 0.70 and Z = 0.02, and start again from 1.6 × 107 K. Before dragging the temperature up towards 3.0 × 107 K, predict where the CNO cycle overtakes the proton–proton chain.

4 · A star poor in metals

The sim is set to a central temperature of 2.0 × 107 K, where the two lines cross for X = 0.70 and Z = 0.02. You will lower Z tenfold, to 0.002, as in an old star poor in metals. Before changing Z, predict where the crossing moves. Then change Z and drag the temperature to find the new crossing.

5 · Less hydrogen in the core

The sim is set back to Z = 0.02 and a central temperature of 2.0 × 107 K, where the two rates are equal for X = 0.70. You will lower X to 0.35, as happens when half the hydrogen in the core has been turned into helium. Before changing X, predict which process supplies the larger share of the energy afterwards.

6 · What the two lines show

Both processes turn four protons into a helium nucleus, but they rise with temperature at very different rates: near these temperatures εpp ∝ T4 and εCNO ∝ T20. So the p–p chain powers the Sun and cooler stars, and above about 2 × 107 K the CNO cycle takes over, as it does in stars more massive than about 1.3 M☉. Fewer metals push the crossing slightly higher; less hydrogen pulls it lower.

The fixed exponents are an approximation: in real stars they fall slowly as T rises, and textbooks quote crossings between about 1.7 and 2 × 107 K, depending on the composition and the rate formulae used.

Two Ways to Burn Hydrogen

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Stars like the Sun turn four protons into one helium nucleus in two different ways: the proton–proton chain and the CNO cycle. This sim plots the energy each one releases per unit mass against the star's central temperature, and lets you change the hydrogen and metal content of the gas.

What you'll learn

  • How each rate depends on temperature, on the hydrogen fraction X and on the metal fraction Z.
  • How to read the share of the energy each process supplies.
  • How far a change in X or Z shifts the balance between them.
The stage: both axes are logarithmic, T runs from 1.0 to 3.0 ×10⁷ K, and the core inset flashes.

What's on screen

  • Yellow line and dot: the proton–proton chain, εpp. Blue line and dot: the CNO cycle, εCNO.
  • Thin vertical line through both dots at the chosen T, and a tick at the centre of the Sun, 1.6×10⁷ K.
  • Faint dashed lines: the previous X or Z, left behind when you change one.
  • Core inset and readouts: the core flashes yellow or blue about ten times a second; the Readouts panel gives T, both rates, their ratio and the CNO share.
See itLook at the stage with the opening settings. Watch for: a yellow line and a blue line, a dot on each at the thin vertical line, and yellow and blue flashes in the core.

03

Two recipes for four protons, with two different rate laws

Both processes turn four protons into one helium-4 nucleus and release 26.7 MeV. The p–p chain starts with two protons meeting. In the CNO cycle one carbon-12 nucleus absorbs four protons in turn, changing into nitrogen and oxygen on the way, emits a helium-4 nucleus and returns as carbon-12 (notes, Fig. 52).

The CNO cycle. Each arrow is a proton capture (p, γ), a positron decay, or the final (p, ⁴He) step. The orange arrow is the slowest.

Every capture has to get through the Coulomb barrier of a nucleus with six or seven protons, and the slowest is proton capture by nitrogen-14. The cycle runs at a rate proportional to the catalysts, that is to Z. Near the temperature of the Sun's centre (notes, 4.65):

εpp ∝ ρ X² T⁴     εCNO ∝ ρ X Z T²⁰
Equation (4.65). Both lines in the sim are drawn in units of εpp at the Sun's centre, so ρ drops out.
Key idea. The p–p chain needs two protons, so it goes as X². The CNO cycle needs one proton and a catalyst, so it goes as X Z.
See itLook at both rates at the Sun-centre temperature, 1.6×10⁷ K, with X = 0.70 and Z = 0.02. Watch for: the yellow dot at 1.00, the blue dot far below it, and flashes that are mostly yellow.
04

A 10% rise in T multiplies the p–p rate by 1.46 and the CNO rate by 6.7

Near a given temperature a rate follows a power law, ⟨σv⟩ ∝ Tζ, with ζ = d ln⟨σv⟩/d ln T (4.63). The Gamow exponent τG, which measures the barrier, sets it:

ζ = (τG − 2) / 3
Equation (4.64).

For two protons at the Sun's centre τG ≈ 13 and ζ ≈ 4. For a proton on nitrogen-14, τG ≈ 60 and ζ ≈ 20. A rise of 10% in T multiplies a rate ∝ Tζ by 1.1ζ: 1.1⁴ = 1.46 for the chain and 1.1²⁰ = 6.7 for the cycle.

The same 10% rise in T on the log axis. The slopes are the exponents, so the CNO rise is five times as tall (20/4 = 5).
Key idea. A taller Coulomb barrier means a steeper rate: a small rise in T changes the CNO rate far more than the p–p rate.
See itRaise T by 10%, from 1.6×10⁷ to 1.76×10⁷ K, at X = 0.70 and Z = 0.02. Watch for: both dots rising, the yellow one a little (εpp: 1.00 to 1.46) and the blue one almost sevenfold (εCNO: 0.0281 to 0.189).
05

The steeper CNO line must cross the p–p line

Dividing the two rates in (4.65) cancels ρ and one factor of X, and leaves T20/T4 = T16. The sim calibrates the ratio to 1 at T = 2.0×10⁷ K for X = 0.70, Z = 0.02:

εCNO / εpp = (Z / 0.02) (0.70 / X) (T / 2.0×10⁷ K)¹⁶
Calibration of the ratio used by the sim.

The CNO share is εCNO / (εpp + εCNO), and each flash in the core is blue with that probability. Where the lines cross the ratio is 1 and the share is 50%. At 1.6×10⁷ K the ratio is 0.8¹⁶ = 0.028, a share of 2.7%.

Both rates against T at X = 0.70, Z = 0.02. Two straight lines on log axes: the blue one is steeper and meets the yellow one.
T Z X

These sliders move the sim too. The numbers come from the sim's own rate function.

See itPut T on the crossing for your current X and Z. Watch for: the two dots sitting on top of each other, and the CNO share close to 50%.
See itSweep T from 1.0 up to 3.0×10⁷ K, at X = 0.70 and Z = 0.02. Watch for: the blue dot climbing past the yellow one near 2.0×10⁷ K, and the flashes turning from mostly yellow to mostly blue.
06

Composition shifts the crossing only a little

Setting the ratio to 1 in the calibrated formula gives the crossing temperature:

Tx = 2.0×10⁷ K × [ (0.02 / Z)(X / 0.70) ]1/16

The 1/16 power makes the crossing insensitive to Z. A tenfold drop to Z = 0.002, as in an old star poor in metals, multiplies Tx only by 101/16 = 1.15, to about 2.3×10⁷ K. At 2.0×10⁷ K the CNO share falls from 50% to 9.1%.

X enters differently: εpp ∝ X² but εCNO ∝ X, so the ratio goes as 1/X. Halving X from 0.70 to 0.35, as when half the core hydrogen has become helium, doubles the ratio. At 2.0×10⁷ K the CNO share rises from 50% to 67%, and the crossing moves down to about 1.9×10⁷ K.

Key idea. Z scales the CNO rate directly, but because the ratio grows as T¹⁶ a big change in Z moves the crossing by a small factor in T.
See itStart at 2.0×10⁷ K with X = 0.70, then lower Z from 0.02 to 0.002. Watch for: the CNO share dropping from 50% to 9.1% while a faint dashed line marks the old blue line.
See itStart at 2.0×10⁷ K with Z = 0.02, then lower X from 0.70 to 0.35. Watch for: both rates falling, the blue one less, so the CNO share rises from 50% to 67%.
07

Where it matters

  • The Sun. At its centre the p–p chain supplies nearly all the energy. The sim's share there, 2.7%, is larger than the Sun's total of about 1%, because the rest of the core is cooler.
  • Stars more massive than about 1.3 M☉. Their centres reach about 2×10⁷ K, where the CNO cycle takes over (notes, 4.4).
  • Convective cores. With such a steep rate, CNO energy release is concentrated near the centre, which is why these stars have convective cores.
  • A thermostat. A small rise in central T raises the rate a lot, so the star expands and cools until the rate falls back. Hydrogen burning on the main sequence is stable.
Go deeper: the exponents 4 and 20 are local

Since τG ∝ T−1/3, ζ itself falls as T rises. For proton plus nitrogen-14 (EG ≈ 45 MeV) it is about 19.5 at 1.6×10⁷ K, 18.0 at 2.0×10⁷ K and 15.7 at 3.0×10⁷ K. The sim holds the exponents at 4 and 20, so its lines stay straight, and it calibrates the crossing to 2.0×10⁷ K. Textbooks quote it between about 1.7 and 2×10⁷ K, depending on composition and rate formulae.

08

Summary

In one line. Both processes turn four protons into helium, but their rates follow different power laws in T, so which one supplies the energy depends on T, Z and X.
  • εpp ∝ ρ X² T⁴ and εCNO ∝ ρ X Z T²⁰ near 1.6×10⁷ K (4.65).
  • A 10% rise in T multiplies them by 1.46 and 6.7; the ratio goes as T¹⁶.
  • CNO share: 2.7% at 1.6×10⁷ K, 50% at 2.0×10⁷ K (X = 0.70, Z = 0.02).
  • Across the sim's ranges of Z and X the crossing moves by at most about 15% in T.

Common mix-ups

  • "Both make one helium nucleus, so each supplies about half." At 1.6×10⁷ K the CNO share is 2.7%.
  • "Catalysts are never used up, so the cycle runs as fast as it likes." Each capture still has to tunnel into a nucleus with six or seven protons.
  • "Ten times less metal means a ten times hotter crossing." The ratio grows as T¹⁶, so the crossing rises by 101/16 = 1.15.

Things to try on your own

  • Set T = 2.5×10⁷ K with X = 0.70 and Z = 0.02. The CNO share should read 97.3%.
  • Set Z = 0.04 at T = 1.6×10⁷ K. The ratio should double, to 0.0563.
  • With X = 0.35 and Z = 0.02, drag T until the share reads 50%. You should find about 1.9×10⁷ K.
